title: Fire on Carmel (1 Kings 18)
hook: Elijah on Mount Carmel, where Carmelites later trace their roots

segments.voice: Yesterday, a widow in Zarephath, a handful of flour, and a pot that never ran dry. Your line was the jar did not fail. What did you give from the bottom of the pot? Day four hundred ten.

The third year of the drought. The fields are dust. King Ahab calls Elijah the troubler of Israel, and Elijah answers: it's you who troubled Israel, by following Baal. Then he makes a proposal. Gather everyone on Mount Carmel, the ridge above the sea. Bring the prophets of Baal, four hundred and fifty of them. And there, in front of the whole nation, we'll settle it. Two altars, two bulls, no fire. Each side calls on its God. The God who answers by fire, he is God. And the people, the Douay-Rheims says, answered: "A very good proposal."
screen: `THE THIRD YEAR OF DROUGHT.` → `EVERYONE TO MOUNT CARMEL.` → `THE GOD WHO ANSWERS BY FIRE.`

segments.voice: Before any fire, Elijah turns to the crowd, and that's where today's line comes from. In the Douay: "How long do you halt between two sides? if the Lord be God, follow him." To halt is to limp. Some readers hear in the Hebrew someone hobbling back and forth between two paths, never putting full weight on either. The people had not quite rejected the God of Israel. They just kept Baal on the side, in case. And the text says they answered him not a word. Then the contest. The prophets of Baal call from morning till noon, and there is no voice, no answer. Elijah rebuilds the Lord's broken-down altar with twelve stones, one for each tribe, and has it soaked with water, three times, until the trench overflows. Then he prays, simply: let this people know that thou art the Lord God, and that thou hast turned their heart again. And the fire of the Lord falls, and burns up the offering, the wood, the stones, even the water in the trench. The people fall on their faces: the Lord he is God. Then Elijah climbs to the top of Carmel, puts his face between his knees, and sends his servant to look at the sea seven times. On the seventh: a little cloud, like a man's foot. Then the rain. Here's the Catholic thread. Centuries later, hermits settled on Mount Carmel, tradition says near a spring named for Elijah. They became the Carmelites, the order of Saint Teresa of Avila, Saint John of the Cross and Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, and they honor Elijah as their spiritual father. Carmelite tradition even saw in that little rising cloud a figure of Mary.
screen: `HOW LONG WILL YOU LIMP?` · `NO VOICE FROM MORNING TILL NOON.` · `FIRE ON A SOAKED ALTAR.` · `HERMITS ON CARMEL: THE CARMELITES.` · then, large: `THE LORD HE IS GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray on a hill or high place. If you can, go somewhere higher than usual: a hill, a top-floor window, a staircase landing, even a step. If you can't, picture Carmel: the ridge, the sea below. Settle, and breathe. Then ask yourself Elijah's question: where am I limping between two sides? Something you half believe, half hedge on. Don't answer it out loud yet. Just notice where your weight is. If you pray, you can do as Elijah did, face down or head bowed, and wait. The bell holds the time.
Fire on Carmel. Elijah's contest on the mountain, where the Lord answered by fire, and where the Carmelites later found their roots. Today's word.
Your line: how long will you halt. Today, pick one thing you've been undecided about for too long, and put your full weight down on one side. Day four hundred ten.

howItsDone: Carmelite friars, nuns and lay Carmelites honor Elijah as their spiritual father and keep his feast, and Catholics who wear the brown scapular do so in honor of Our Lady of Mount Carmel.

original.note: Hebrew: Carmel, garden land or orchard. The ridge gave its name to the Carmelite order.

trapdoor: what you thought: a showdown about whose god has better fire.
what it means: Elijah calls a hedging people to stop limping between two sides, and the Lord answers so that their heart may turn back.

what a scholar hears: the Hebrew for halt is a word for limping, which some translators gloss as hopping between two branches; and Carmelite tradition later read the little cloud from the sea as a figure of Mary.

sources.quoted: How long do you halt between two sides? if the Lord be God, follow him

sources.ref: Carmelite tradition; Rule of Saint Albert (c. 1206–1214)

notes: The killing of the prophets of Baal at the Kishon (18:40) is omitted. Elijah's mockery (18:27) is also omitted. Keeper to decide whether either should be acknowledged.
Carmelite origins: Latin hermits on Mount Carmel in the late 12th / early 13th century, given a rule by Albert of Jerusalem (c. 1206–1214). Confirm 'late twelfth century'.
Feast of Saint Elijah on July 20 is kept in the Carmelite calendar; Our Lady of Mount Carmel on July 16. Confirm.
The Carmelite reading of the little cloud (18:44) as a figure of Mary is a traditional one; confirm.
The carry ('how long will you halt') blends KJV ('How long halt ye') and Douay ('How long do you halt'). Hebrew posechim al shtei hasse'ippim; 'two branches/crutches' is a common gloss. Confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): 'three years without rain' changed to 'the third year' (18:1 says the third year; Luke 4:25 gives three years and six months); cut 'late twelfth century' and the July 16/20 feast dates (claims rule); Hebrew 'limping' gloss now attributed to some readers. Keeper: confirm the Carmelite spring tradition.
